analytic.title: The Global Feasibility and Schedulability of General Task Models on Multiprocessor Platforms *

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Feasibility analysis determines (prior to system execution-time) whether a specified collection of hard-realtime jobs executed on a processing platform can meet all deadlines. In this paper, we derive near-optimal sufficient tests for determining whether a given collection of jobs can feasibly meet all deadlines upon a specified multiprocessor platform assuming job migration is permitted. These tests are general enough to be applied even when the collection of jobs is incompletely specified. We discuss the applicability of these tests to the scheduling of collections of jobs that are generated by systems of recurrent real-time tasks. We also show that our feasibility conditions may be used to obtain global-EDF schedulability conditions.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Recent research efforts on the formal analysis of general task models executed upon multiprocessor systems have focused on feasibility analysis. Feasibility analysis determines whether a specified hard-real-time system can be executed in a manner that all deadlines are met. Currently, for general real-time task models, a complete characterization of task systems as either feasible or infeasible is unknown. However, prior work has been able to obtain a partial characterization; Baker and Cirinei [2] have recently proposed a demand-based metric for identifying infeasible task systems on a multiprocessor platform. For feasibility, we derived conditions [5] for identifying task systems that are feasible on multiprocessors under certain migration restrictions. However, there exists a "gap" (or set of task systems) for which no existing test can correctly categorize as either "feasible" or "infeasible." The goal of the work reported in this paper is to minimize this gap of uncertainty for a wide range of task models on multiprocessor platforms; reducing this gap of uncertainty is important for our theoretical understanding of multiprocessor real-time systems and has important implications for multiprocessor scheduling algorithms (e.g. see [12] for a thorough discussion on the implications of feasibility to scheduling). Towards this goal of obtaining a more complete characterization, we derive in this paper a much more accurate multiprocessor feasibility test than previous tests, prove that our tests narrow the gap of uncertainty to within a constant factor of the optimal test, and discuss the implications of our feasibility tests to recurrent task models and global-EDF scheduling.

In this paper, we assume that a hard-real-time instance I is represented as a collection of jobs. Each job is characterized by three parameters -an arrival time, an execution requirement, and a deadline -with the interpretation that it needs to execute for an amount equal to its execution requirement between its arrival time and its deadline. We focus on migratory, preemptive systems; that is, we permit that an executing job may be preempted at any instant and have its execution resumed later on the same or different processor, at no additional cost or penalty. Since migration and preemption costs are affected by the properties of the particular scheduling algorithm and our focus is on the feasibility of the task system (irrespective of scheduling algorithm), determining the effect of migration and preemption is beyond the scope of this paper.

In many systems, a complete specification of the realtime instance I (i.e. knowledge of all three parameters for each job of I) may not always be possible prior to system execution. In particular, the system designer may not know a priori the arrival-time of each job in the system; instead, the designer may only have partial arrival-time information and a bound on the maximum job inter-arrival rate. For such systems, feasibility and schedulability analysis algorithms for completely specified systems are not applicable. Furthermore, many current formal models of systems comprised of repeatedly executing processes (modelled as realtime tasks) do not permit the complete specification of job attributes. For example, the sporadic task model [9,6] does not specify the arrival-time of jobs of a task, but only specifies that the arrival times of successive jobs of a task be at least a specified time-interval apart. Many other models for real-time tasks have also been proposed, including the Liu and Layland model [8], the multiframe model [10], the generalized multiframe model [4], and a more general DAG-based model [3]. While each such task modelled in these formal models can guarantee minimum inter-arrival separations between successive jobs, the exact arrival times of individual jobs is only revealed during run-time.

The research reported in this document focuses on obtaining sufficient conditions for feasibility and schedulability analysis based on real-time workload characterizations which may be obtained for general task models (both completely and partially specified systems, including all task models mentioned in the preceding paragraph). In particular, we focus on a workload characterizations that may be determined prior to system run-time, and that can be efficiently determined given systems representation as a collection of recurrent tasks. The results obtained for this report focus on migratory scheduling (see [5] for feasibility results for non-migratory scheduling).

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we formally describe our job and processor models. In Section 3, we discuss the context of our results and prior work on schedulability of real-time instances. In Section 4, we obtain sufficient conditions for multiprocessor feasibility and schedulability analysis of real-time instances. In Section 5, we describe how certain system parameters, upon which our feasibility-analysis algorithm depends, may be computed for real-time systems that are specified using various popular models for recurrent processes, such as the Liu and Layland or the sporadic task models. In Section 6, we prove the feasibility condition presented in Section 4.

div.head: Workload and processor models
div.p: We characterize a real-time job J i by three parameters: an arrival time A i , an execution requirement E i , and a relative deadline D i , with the interpretation that J i must execute for E i time units over the time interval [A i , A i + D i ). The interval [A i , A i + D i ) is referred to as J i 's activation period. We denote a real-time instance I as a finite or infinite collection of jobs I = {J 1 , J 2 , . . .}. For the remainder of the paper, we will assume that jobs are indexed in order of their absolute deadline (i.e. for J i , J j ∈ I, i ≤ j if and only if
div.formula: A i + D i ≤ A j + D j ).
div.p: We will assume that we are given a multiprocessor Π comprised of m identical processors, Π = {π 1 , π 2 , . . . , π m }. We assume (without loss of generality) that the execution requirement E i of each job of I has been normalized with respect to a unit-speed processor. The model of scheduling we consider allows for processor preemption with migration (recall from Section 1 that we assume preemption and migration have zero additional execution cost).

Let us define the demand of a real-time instance over a time interval to be the sum of the execution requirements of all jobs in the instance, that have both their arrival times and their deadlines within the interval:
div.formula: demand(I, t 1 , t 2 ) def = (J i ∈I)∧(t 1 ≤A i )∧(A i +D i ≤t 2 ) E i (1)
div.p: For any real-time instance I, we define its density and load as follows:
div.formula: density(I) def = max J i ∈I (E i /D i ) ( 2 ) load(I) def = max t 1 <t 2 demand(I, t 1 , t 2 ) t 2 -t 1(3)
div.p: Intuitively, density(I) represents the maximum computational demand of any individual job, and load(I) the maximum cumulative computational demand of any subset of the set of jobs, in the real-time instance I.

div.head: Context and Prior Work
div.p: Exact polynomial-time algorithms for both migratory and non-migratory feasibility-analysis are known (via network-flow techniques), when all characteristics of all the jobs in an instance are known during the time that feasibility analysis is being performed. We refer to such instances, where the arrival time, execution time, and deadline of each job is known prior to run-time, as completely specified instances. However, in order to more flexibly support dynamic and non-static systems, many real-time systems model the real-time workload as collections of recurrent (such as Liu and Layland or sporadic) tasks; in these models, it is not possible to know beforehand what realtime instance will be generated by the system during runtime. In fact, different runs of the same system may result in different real-time instances being generated; in general, any given collection of recurrent real-time tasks may legally generate infinitely many different real-time instances, each of which satisfies the constraints placed on their generation by the recurrent tasks. Also, each such real-time instance may have infinitely many jobs, which means that feasibilityanalysis algorithms that need to examine all the jobs in the instance cannot possible be applied.

In this paper, we present feasibility and schedulability conditions for the analysis of real-time instances I for which complete specifications need not be known, provided upper bounds on density(I) and load(I) are a priori known. We will refer to such real-time instances as partially specified instances; as we will see in Section 5, tight bounds on load and density can be efficiently determined for all instances generated by collections of recurrent real-time tasks represented in a wide range of formal models.

In [5], we related feasibility with load and density. In particular, it was shown that both density ≤ 1 and load ≤ m are necessary conditions for feasibility on an identical multiprocessor platform comprised of m unit-capacity processors: In addition, feasibility conditions for migratory and nonmigratory scheduling were obtained: Theorem 1 (from [5]) If I denotes a real-time instance satisfying

div.head: Lemma 1 (from [5]) If real-time instance I is feasible on an identical multiprocessor platform comprised of m unitcapacity processors, it must be the case that
div.formula: load(I) ≤ max 1, 1 3 m -(m -1)density(I) , (4
div.p: then I is (migratory and non-migratory) feasible on a platform comprised of m unit-capacity processors.

The results contained in this report improve upon these sufficient feasibility analysis conditions for migratory scheduling, and introduce schedulability conditions based on load and density for edf scheduling. Our results are complimentary to the work of [2] which focuses on necessary conditions for feasibility using a metric similar to load.

An alternative characterization of real-time workload that has been proposed is the synthetic utilization [1] of a task instance. Lemma 1 helps explain why we have chosen to not use this characterization rather than the load, density abstraction. Lemma 1 demonstrates that m is an upper bound on the load of any instance feasible upon m unit-capacity processors; however, there is no corresponding upper bound on the synthetic utilization of feasible instances 1 . In obtaining a bound (as we do in Theorem 2 below) such that any instance with load no larger than this bound is guaranteed feasible, we also obtain some measure of the relative efficacy or "goodness" of this bound since we know that all instances with load greater than m are guaranteed infeasible. Since there is no upper bound on synthetic utilization of feasible instances, no such relative goodness can be deduced for a synthetic utilization bound.

div.head: Summary of results
div.p: In this section, we summarize the results that we have obtained for the feasibility and schedulability analysis of real-time instance I. The results we have obtained are sufficient conditions for feasibility and schedulability in terms of the load and density characterization. Section 5 discusses the tightness of the feasibility result and the implications to recurrent task models. Proof of the feasibility results described in this section are delayed until Section 6.

Specifically, we had set out to obtain a feasibility region in the two-dimensional space [0, 1] × [0, m], such that any instance I with density(I) and load(I) lying in this region is guaranteed to be feasible. div.head: Schedulability
div.p: Phillips et al. [12] related the concept of multiprocessor feasibility with edf schedulability using a technique known as resource augmentation. Specifically, they proved that any real-time instance I feasible on a platform with m unitcapacity processors is schedulable according to edf on processing platform with m processors each of speed (2 -1 m ). The following schedulability condition is immediately obtained from Theorem 2 and using a resource augmentation speed-up result of [12].

div.head: Theorem 3 For real-time instance I and identical multiprocessor platform Π comprised of m unit-speed processors, if
div.formula: load(I) < max 1, m -ρ(m -2)density(I) ρ(1 + ρ • density(I)) (8
div.p: where ρ = 2 -1 m , then the earliest-deadline-first scheduling algorithm (edf) can successfully schedule I upon Π.

div.head: Application of Results to Recurrent Task Models
div.p: The feasibility-approach algorithm in Section 4 above requires that load parameter load(I) and the density parameter density(I) of the real-time instance I being analyzed be known. As we had argued in the introduction, many realtime systems are comprised of collections of independent recurrent real-time tasks, each of which generates a potentially infinite sequence of jobs. Given the specifications of such a real-time system, we now discuss the issue of determining bounds on the load parameter of any real-time instance that could be generated by this system during runtime (the density parameter can be in most cases trivially determined). Our approach is based upon the concept of the demand bound function (dbf) of recurrent real-time tasks; in the next subsection, we describe this concept and explain how it relates to determining load Ṫhe feasibility and schedulability bounds obtained in this paper may be directly applied to such recurrent task systems, provided that there is no assumption of FCFS execution for overlapping jobs of the same task.

div.head: The dbf abstraction
div.p: We start out with a definition of the demand bound function:

div.head: Definition 1 (Demand Bound Function) Let τ i denote a recurrent real-time task, and t a non-negative real-number. The demand bound function dbf(τ i , t) denotes the maximum cumulative execution requirement that could be generated by jobs of τ i that have both ready times and deadlines within any time interval of duration t.
div.p: The demand bound function is efficiently determined for all the recurring real-time task models mentioned in this paper; algorithms for doing so for the Liu and Layland and sporadic task models are to be found in [6], for the multiframe and generalized multiframe models in [4], and for the DAG-based model in [3]. As an illustrative example, we present without proof the formula for computing dbf for a task specified according to the sporadic task model -a proof may be found in [6]. Let a sporadic task τ i be represented by the 3-tuple (e i , d i , p i ), with the interpretation that this task generates an infinite sequence of jobs each with execution requirement e i and relative deadline d i , and with the arrival times of successive jobs separated by at least p i time units. For such a task,
div.formula: dbf(τ i , t) def = max 0, t -d i p i + 1 × e i
div.p: Given that we know how to determine the dbf for many of the important recurrent real-time task models, we now discuss how to compute bounds on the value of load(I) for any real-time instance I that is generated by a collection of recurrent real-time tasks τ = {τ 1 , τ 2 , . . .}.
Let I denote any real-time instance that is generated during run-time by a collection of recurrent real-time tasks τ.
The maximum cumulative execution requirement by jobs in I over any time interval [t 1 , t 2 ) is bounded from above by the sum of the maximum execution requirements of the individual tasks in τ:
div.formula: demand(I, t 1 , t 2 ) ≤ ( τ i ∈τ dbf(τ i , t 2 -t 1 )) .

The above bound is tight (in the sense that there exists a instance I generated by task system τ with load(I) equal to the rhs of Equation 9) when the different tasks comprising τ are completely independent of one another. This requirement is formalized in the task independence assumptions [4]. We briefly review these independence assumptions below; a more complete discussion may be found in [4].
There are two requirements that are satisfied by systems satisfying the task independence assumptions:

1. The runtime behavior of a task does not depend upon the behavior of other tasks in the system. That is, each task is an independent entity, perhaps driven by separate external events. It is not permissible for one task to generate a job directly in response to another task generating a job.
2. The workload constraints can be specified without making any references to "absolute" time. That is, specifications such as "Task τ i generates a job at timeinstant 3" are forbidden.

The task independence assumptions are extremely general and are satisfied by a wide variety of the kinds of task systems one may encounter in practice. Most common task models, including the Liu and Layland [8], multiframe [10] generalized multiframe [4], and the DAG-based model [3], satisfy these assumptions. The reader is referred to [5,4] for a more complete discussion of the task independence assumption and to [5] for a discussion of how to efficiently compute the feasibility and schedulability of a recurrent task system from Theorems 2 and 3.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: While feasibility and schedulability analysis on preemptive uniprocessors is well understood, analysis of multiprocessor systems for general task models has received less attention. In this paper, we have focused on obtaining both feasibility and schedulability conditions on a multiprocessor platform in terms of the load and density workload characterization. We have considered an extremely general task model, characterized by the task independence assumption; therefore, our results are applicable to all task systems satisfying this assumption. To the best of our knowledge, the schedulability test contained in this paper represents the first known result for the migratory scheduling of general recurrent tasks (i.e. generalized multiframe and DAG-based model) on a multiprocessor platform. The feasibility results are an improvement of prior results we have obtained for migratory scheduling.
